specPoints.text: be able to select and justify a suitable experimental technique to obtain rate data for a given reaction, including: i titration ii colorimetry iii mass change iv volume of gas evolved v other suitable technique(s) for a given reaction

primer.text: Every rate measurement leans on a property that changes as the reaction proceeds and is proportional to a concentration. This note surveys the laboratory toolkit: colorimetry for colour change, mass loss for dense gases, gas collection for volume change, and titration with quenching for concentration itself, each with its suitability limits and sketch-graph reading.

lessons.title: Following rate by colour: colorimetry
lessons.opening: When a reaction changes colour, a colorimeter turns that change into concentration data. Light passes through the mixture, a detector logs the intensity reaching it every few seconds, and the plotted readings trace how reactants and products move with time. Precipitates spoil the method by scattering light.
keyPoints: A colorimeter measures the amount of light passing through a solution, logged every few seconds.
The light intensity reaching the detector is related to concentration, so the plotted data represent concentration against time.
For a coloured reactant the colour intensity fades with time; the sketch graph shows intensity falling.
Colorimetry cannot follow the formation of coloured precipitates, because suspended particles scatter or block the light.

low.restatement: The colorimeter logs light intensity every few seconds; since intensity tracks concentration, the plot is a concentration-time curve, and precipitates break it.
low.analogy: Watching milk dissolve into tea through a clear mug: the clearer the view, the further the mixing has gone.
low.examPointer: Name the interference problem - scattering by suspended solid - when asked why colorimetry fails for precipitates.

medium.restatement: Absorbance and concentration walk together, so a detector reading is a concentration proxy; the method's one weakness is optical, not chemical.
medium.analogy: Headlights in fog: the denser the fog between you and the lamp, the less light arrives, and any floating debris blurs everything.
medium.examPointer: If a question shows a calibration curve, use it to convert absorbance readings into concentrations before quoting rates.

check.stem: A colorimeter determines rate by measuring

options.text: The amount of light passing through the solution at intervals
options.explanation: Falling or rising light intensity tracks concentration change.

options.text: The mass of the reaction vessel
options.explanation: Mass belongs to the mass-loss method.
Volume belongs to the gas-collection method.
Temperature is controlled, not measured as the rate signal.

check.stem: The plotted detector readings represent concentration against time because

options.text: Light intensity reaching the detector is related to the concentration of the coloured species
options.explanation: Absorbance and concentration move together, making intensity a proxy.
Different quantities entirely.
No such heating is involved.

options.text: Colour is always independent of concentration
options.explanation: The method relies on the opposite.

check.stem: Colorimetry is unsuitable for a reaction that forms a coloured precipitate because

options.text: Suspended particles scatter or block the light, corrupting the intensity reading
options.explanation: The optical path degrades, so intensity no longer tracks concentration cleanly.
Speed is not the problem.
No such dissolving occurs.

options.text: The detector cannot see any colour at all
options.explanation: Colour is visible; the trouble is scattering.

check.stem: For a coloured reactant monitored by colorimetry, the sketch graph of colour intensity against time

options.text: Falls as the reactant is used up
options.explanation: The coloured species is consumed, so intensity drops.
A reactant's colour cannot rise while it is consumed.
A horizontal line would mean no reaction.
Clean kinetics data smooth such noise.

check.stem: Detector readings are taken every few seconds so that

options.text: Enough points exist to draw a smooth concentration-time curve and read gradients
options.explanation: Frequent sampling gives the curve its shape.
Lamp life is irrelevant to sampling.
Sampling does not alter kinetics.
One reading cannot yield a rate.

check.stem: State what a colorimeter measures and how often readings are taken.
check.modelAnswer: It measures the light intensity passing through the solution, logged every few seconds.

check.stem: State the limitation that stops colorimetry following precipitate formation.
check.modelAnswer: Coloured precipitates scatter or block the light, so the detector reading no longer represents concentration.

check.stem: Explain why light intensity can stand in for concentration in colorimetry.
check.modelAnswer: The colour of a solution deepens with the concentration of the coloured species, so the light absorbed, and therefore the intensity reaching the detector, changes in step with concentration.

check.stem: A reaction turns a clear solution progressively yellow. Describe how you would obtain a rate graph from this mixture.
check.modelAnswer: Run the mixture in a colorimeter, log the rising absorbance of the yellow species every few seconds, convert absorbance to concentration with a calibration curve, and plot concentration against time.

lessons.title: Following rate by mass loss
lessons.opening: When a reaction releases a dense gas, the escaping gas carries mass out of the vessel, and a balance records the loss. Carbon dioxide from marble and acid is the classic case; hydrogen is too light for the method to resolve.
keyPoints: When a gas escapes from a reaction vessel the total mass decreases, and the decrease can be recorded with a balance.
Calcium carbonate reacting with hydrochloric acid gives off carbon dioxide; the mass is recorded every few seconds and plotted.
Mass loss measures the amount of reactant-side material lost, so the graph reads as an amount-of-reactant against time curve.
The gas must be dense enough for a 2 or 3 decimal-place balance: carbon dioxide (Mr = 44) suits the method, hydrogen (Mr = 2) does not.

low.restatement: Gas escaping removes mass; weigh every few seconds and plot the loss - but only dense gases such as CO2 register on a normal balance.
low.analogy: A shopper standing on scales while unloading oranges: each bag carried off shows as a small drop, but unloading rice grains one by one would not register.
low.examPointer: Quote the Mr comparison - CO2 at 44 works, H2 at 2 fails - when justifying the method's limits.

medium.restatement: The balance is a concentration proxy: every gram lost is gas that has formed and left, so the falling mass curve is the reaction's progress line.
medium.analogy: An hourglass read from the empty chamber: the sand that has passed is exactly what the top has lost.
medium.examPointer: State the density condition before choosing this method in a plan question.

check.stem: Mass loss can follow a reaction rate only when

options.text: A gas is produced that is dense enough to register on the balance
options.explanation: The method's resolution depends on a substantial mass change.
Colour is the colorimetry signal.
Precipitates stay in the vessel and do not change the mass.
Enthalpy plays no role here.

check.stem: In the calcium carbonate and hydrochloric acid experiment, the mass decreases because

options.text: Carbon dioxide escapes from the vessel as the reaction proceeds
options.explanation: The gaseous product leaves, taking its mass with it.
Evaporation is not the intended cause.
The solid converts to products, some of which escape as gas.
A calibrated balance does not drift by design.

check.stem: Hydrogen is a poor gas for the mass-loss method because

options.text: Its molar mass of 2 makes the mass change too small for a 2 or 3 dp balance
options.explanation: The lost mass per mole is tiny, so readings barely move.
No such reaction occurs.
Hydrogen is colourless, which is irrelevant here.

options.text: It dissolves completely in the acid
options.explanation: Dissolution is not the stated limitation.

check.stem: The graph of mass loss against time is equivalent to a graph of

options.explanation: Mass lost measures how much material has reacted away.

options.text: Amount of product present in the vessel
options.explanation: The gaseous product has left, so it is not present to measure.
Temperature is not plotted here.

options.text: Concentration of the gas inside the vessel
options.explanation: The gas escapes, so its internal concentration is not what the balance reads.

check.stem: Mass readings are taken every few seconds during the experiment in order to

options.text: Give enough points to plot the mass-time curve and read the rate from its gradient
options.explanation: Rate comes from the slope of the plotted curve.
Calibration is separate from sampling.
Weighing does not warm anything.
The whole method is graphical.

check.stem: State which gas is suitable for the mass-loss method and which is not.
check.modelAnswer: Carbon dioxide (Mr = 44) is dense enough for the method; hydrogen (Mr = 2) is not.

check.stem: State what is plotted in the mass-loss method.
check.modelAnswer: The change in mass of the vessel and contents, measured every few seconds, plotted against time.

check.stem: Explain why the mass-loss graph doubles as a reactant-amount graph.
check.modelAnswer: Each gram of mass lost is exactly the gas that has formed from the reactants and left the vessel, so the cumulative loss measures how much reactant material has been consumed by that moment.

check.stem: A student proposes the mass-loss method for magnesium reacting with dilute acid to give hydrogen. Evaluate the proposal.
check.modelAnswer: Hydrogen's molar mass of 2 makes the mass change too small for a balance reading to 2 or 3 decimal places, so the proposal is weak; a gas syringe measuring the hydrogen volume is the better choice.

lessons.title: Following rate by gas volume
lessons.opening: Trapping a product gas and reading its volume over time is the most standard rate method. A gas syringe collects the gas directly, or an inverted measuring cylinder over water works when the gas is not water soluble. Magnesium in acid giving hydrogen is the canonical example.
keyPoints: Trapping a product gas and tracking its volume over time supplies the rate data.
Magnesium reacting with hydrochloric acid to release hydrogen is the standard gas-volume example.
A gas syringe gathers the gas directly; the alternative apparatus bubbles it through water into an inverted measuring cylinder, workable whenever the gas dissolves poorly in water.
The volume measured every few seconds plots as a graph of volume against time, and the volume represents the amount of product formed.

low.restatement: Collect the gas (syringe, or inverted cylinder over water for non-soluble gases), read volume every few seconds, plot volume against time.
low.analogy: Filling a party balloon from a fizzy drink: the balloon's size tracks how much gas has escaped the bottle.
low.examPointer: The dissolved-in-water caveat is the examiner's favourite caveat - state it when choosing the inverted-cylinder option.

medium.restatement: Gas volume is the product side's ruler: each cubic centimetre collected corresponds to a fixed number of moles formed, so the volume-time curve is a product-amount curve.
medium.analogy: A milometer for gas: every turn of the wheel adds a fixed distance, and the total says how far the reaction has travelled.
medium.examPointer: Remember the volume axis reads amount of product, not reactant remaining.

check.stem: The gas-volume method measures rate by

options.text: Trapping the product gas and recording its volume at intervals
options.explanation: Growing volume marks product formation over time.
That is the mass-loss method.
That is the colorimetry method.
That is the quenching route of the next lesson.

check.stem: The alternative set-up bubbles gas through water into an inverted measuring cylinder, but only when

options.text: The gas is not water soluble
options.explanation: Dissolution would steal gas from the measured volume.
Colour is irrelevant to collection.

options.text: The gas is denser than air
options.explanation: Density against air does not govern this set-up.
Enthalpy plays no role in the choice.

check.stem: In the magnesium and hydrochloric acid example, the gas collected is

options.explanation: Magnesium plus acid liberates hydrogen.
Carbonates give carbon dioxide; magnesium is not a carbonate.
No oxygen is produced by this reaction.
Chloride stays as chloride ions in solution.

check.stem: The graph of gas volume evolved against time represents

options.explanation: Volume collected measures product formed.
Reactant amount is inferred by subtraction, not read directly.
The axes are volume and time.
Temperature is not the measured variable.

check.stem: Readings of gas volume are taken every few seconds so that

options.text: A smooth volume-time curve can be plotted and its gradient read as the rate
options.explanation: Gradients need a well-populated curve.

options.text: The gas stays in the syringe
options.explanation: Sampling does not trap the gas.
Reading a volume never changes the chemistry.
Intermediate points carry the rate information.

check.stem: State the two collection arrangements for measuring gas volume.
check.modelAnswer: A gas syringe collecting the gas directly, or an inverted measuring cylinder over water.

check.stem: State the condition for using the inverted measuring cylinder over water.
check.modelAnswer: The gas must not be water soluble, or it would dissolve instead of being collected.

check.stem: Explain why gas volume serves as a stand-in for amount of product.
check.modelAnswer: At a fixed temperature and pressure the volume of a gas is proportional to the number of moles present, so every increment of collected volume corresponds to a fixed amount of product formed.

check.stem: A reaction gives off ammonia, which dissolves readily in water. Which gas-volume arrangement should be avoided, and why?
check.modelAnswer: The inverted measuring cylinder over water should be avoided, because dissolving ammonia would remove gas from the collected volume and understate the rate; a gas syringe is the appropriate choice.

lessons.title: Concentration itself: titration, quenching and clock points
lessons.opening: Measuring concentration during a reaction is awkward because sampling and analysing take time. Quenching freezes a sample so titration can read its concentration; otherwise the clock trick stops the timer at a visible endpoint, such as the moment sulfur hides a cross under the flask.
keyPoints: Measuring concentration changes directly is difficult because taking and analysing a sample can disturb the reaction unless it is deliberately stopped, which is called quenching.
Titration of a quenched sample gives its concentration at the moment of quenching.
It is often simpler to stop the clock at a visible point in the reaction, such as when a piece of magnesium has just dissolved.
The sodium thiosulfate and hydrochloric acid reaction slowly forms a yellow sulfur precipitate that obscures a cross seen through the solution, giving a timing point.

low.restatement: Quench a sample, titrate it for concentration; or time a visible endpoint - the disappearing-cross reaction is the standard clock point.
low.analogy: Freezing a film of a race at chosen moments: each frozen frame (quenched sample) can be measured in comfort afterwards.
low.examPointer: Use the word quenching when a question asks how to stop a sample from continuing to react.

medium.restatement: Concentration is the quantity every rate curve secretly plots, so the most direct methods grab it: freeze the chemistry, then measure at leisure.
medium.analogy: Bookmarking pages in a melting ice sculpture: you cannot measure while it melts, so you snap-freeze a copy and read it calmly.
medium.examPointer: For the thiosulfate reaction, say what the observer sees - the cross disappearing - and what that moment means: a fixed small amount of sulfur formed.

check.stem: Quenching a sample means

options.text: Deliberately stopping the reaction in that sample so analysis does not change the reading
options.explanation: A quenched sample is frozen at its quench-moment composition.

options.text: Cooling the sample to room temperature only
options.explanation: Cooling alone does not stop the chemistry.
Dilution is not the definition.
Filtration is not the definition.

check.stem: After quenching, the sample's concentration is obtained by

options.explanation: Titration reads the quenched concentration.
Precipitates defeat colorimetry.
Mass is not concentration.
Gas volume is a different method.

check.stem: The disappearing-cross experiment works because

options.text: The forming sulfur precipitate gradually obscures a cross viewed through the mixture, giving a repeatable endpoint
options.explanation: The visual endpoint is the timing signal.
No magnetism is involved.
Acidity is not the signal.
The cross sits outside the flask; the solution clouds.

check.stem: Stopping the clock at a visible point such as complete dissolution of magnesium is useful because

options.text: It times a fixed extent of reaction without any sampling or titration
options.explanation: A visible endpoint replaces instrumental monitoring.
The clock measures time, not concentration.

options.text: It works for reactions with no visible change
options.explanation: Visibility is the whole requirement.

options.text: It removes the need for a stopwatch
options.explanation: A stopwatch is exactly what is used.

check.stem: Taking a sample for titration without quenching risks

options.text: The reaction continuing in the sample after removal, corrupting the concentration reading
options.explanation: Unquenched samples keep reacting during handling.
Evaporation is not the stated risk.

options.text: The titrant reacting with the flask
options.explanation: The titrant meets the sample, not the flask.
Samples of reacting mixtures are not stable.

check.stem: State what quenching does to a removed sample.
check.modelAnswer: Quenching deliberately stops the reaction in the sample so that its composition is frozen for analysis.

check.stem: Name the observation that signals the endpoint in the thiosulfate-acid clock experiment.
check.modelAnswer: The yellow sulfur precipitate formed obscures a cross viewed through the solution.

check.stem: Explain why titration of an unquenched sample gives an unreliable concentration.
check.modelAnswer: The sample keeps reacting between removal and analysis, so the concentration measured by titration belongs to the analysis moment rather than the removal moment, corrupting the time-concentration pair.

check.stem: A reaction mixture is colourless throughout and gives off no gas. Outline a workable rate measurement plan.
check.modelAnswer: Remove samples at timed intervals, quench each one, and titrate to read concentration; plotting the quenched concentrations against their removal times builds the concentration-time curve.

glossary.definition: Rate measurement by logging the light intensity passing through a coloured solution.
Rate measurement by recording the mass escaping as a dense gas leaves the vessel.
Deliberately stopping a removed sample's reaction so its concentration can be titrated honestly.
A sealed barrel that traps a product gas so its volume can be read against time.
